analysis.one_liner: Requires a 10-cent refundable deposit on beer and soda containers, with unclaimed deposits funding state recycling.
analysis.headline: A national 10-cent deposit on beer and soda cans and bottles drew 68 bipartisan cosponsors but died without a vote in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a 10-cent refund value on every beer, soda, wine cooler, and carbonated water container sold nationwide. Drinkers would get the 10 cents back when they returned the empty container; distributors would pay whatever deposits went unclaimed to the states to fund pollution prevention and recycling. The bill also banned pull-tab cans and barred distributors and retailers from dumping covered containers in landfills. It never advanced past its first subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and local communities. Anyone who returns a container gets the full 10 cents back, so the deposit is only a cost to people who throw empties away. Municipalities gain twice: less litter to collect and fewer beverage containers filling landfills, plus a stream of unclaimed-deposit money for state recycling programs [S3]. States with existing deposit laws or 70% recycling rates are exempt, so the bill sets a floor rather than overriding stronger state systems [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, municipalities, and state recycling programs

how_it_helps.text: Every covered container carries a 10-cent refund value that retailers collect from consumers and must pay back to anyone returning the same brand and container type, making returns pay for the people who do them [S3].
Each year, distributors must pay their states the value of all deposits that went unclaimed, and states must spend that money on pollution prevention and recycling programs [S3].

Distributors must pay returners at least 2 cents per container above the deposit to cover handling, and retailers and distributors are barred from sending covered containers or their metal, glass, or plastic to landfills [S3].

The bill's findings state that existing state deposit laws proved inexpensive to administer and shifted recycling and litter-control costs to beverage producers and consumers, and that a national system would conserve energy and reduce municipal solid-waste costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Beverage producers and distributors, which must administer the deposit system and hand unclaimed deposits to the states; container manufacturers, which face the pull-tab ban and return-system requirements; and grocery and convenience retailers, which must collect deposits, store returned empties, and pay refunds. Consumers who never return containers lose the 10 cents each, effectively making littering more expensive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage makers, distributors, container manufacturers, and retailers

drawbacks.text: Consumers pay 10 cents per container up front and only recover it by returning empties, so people who do not return containers bear a direct cost, and the refund value adjusts upward for inflation every ten years [S3].

Retailers and distributors bear real handling costs — collecting deposits, storing empty containers, and paying refunds — and the guaranteed handling fee (2 cents per container, paid by distributors) may not fully cover them, with costs potentially passed to consumers as higher prices [S3].

The bill covers only beer, malt beverages, mineral water, soda water, wine coolers, and carbonated soft drinks; milk, juice, wine, and liquor containers are excluded, leaving a significant share of container litter outside the system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For everyday people the trade is favorable: a returned container costs nothing, unclaimed deposits become public recycling money, and the bill's own findings cite state experience that deposit systems are cheap to run and relieve communities of litter and disposal costs. The genuine costs fall mostly on the beverage, packaging, and retail industries, with a smaller, avoidable cost on consumers who throw empties away. The main design gap is the exclusion of milk, juice, wine, and liquor containers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee in its first week, and no markup, vote, or further action ever happened before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on April 22, 1993, with more than 60 original cosponsors from both parties [S3].
The bill gathered 68 cosponsors in total — 56 Democrats, 11 Republicans, and 1 Independent [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5].

Eight days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — through the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The beverage, packaging, and retail industries came out ahead: they never had to operate a national deposit system or turn unclaimed deposits over to the states. Municipalities and state recycling programs, which the bill would have funded, continued to bear the costs of container litter and disposal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beverage and packaging makers, and retailers

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Beverage Container Reuse and Recycling Act and recruited 68 cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 68 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 11 Republicans, 56 Democrats, and 1 Independent.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on the day of introduction and to its Transportation and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee eight days later; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled in the two years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Beverage and packaging industry (soft drink makers, brewers, and can and bottle manufacturers)
against.what_they_did: Campaigns by beverage producers, container manufacturers, and retail trade groups helped keep national bottle-deposit bills from reaching floor votes across multiple Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 68 cosponsors split 56 Democrats, 11 Republicans, and 1 Independent, so support crossed party lines; it died in committee rather than on any recorded vote [S4].

industries.industry: Beverage producers and distributors (soft drinks and beer)
industries.note: They would have had to administer the 10-cent deposit system and pay each state the value of every unclaimed deposit. The bill's findings explicitly describe the design as internalizing recycling and litter costs to beverage producers and consumers instead of taxpayers [S3].

industries.industry: Metal, glass, and plastic container manufacturers
industries.note: A nationwide deposit mandate and the ban on pull-tab cans would have reshaped what they sell and required containers built for return and reuse [S3].
They would collect deposits at sale, store returned empties, and pay refunds, bearing storage and handling costs not fully covered by the guaranteed 2-cent handling fee [S3].

industries.industry: State recycling programs and municipal waste services
industries.note: Unclaimed deposits flow to states for pollution prevention and recycling, and municipalities face less litter and lower disposal costs as containers get returned rather than landfilled [S3].
